Pepper Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band Beatles album, 1967. The useful Invasion story — verse, chorus, suit, scream — is already too small by the time it appears. Revolver Beatles album, 1966. One of the records that made “British Invasion” a poor name for what came next. The Rolling Stones Rolling Stones the Stones London R&B group. They kept the Chess debt in the foreground longer than the variety-show version of the Invasion wanted. Mick Jagger Rolling Stones singer. London School of Economics is sometimes mentioned as if it explained the band. The Chess covers explain more. Keith Richards Rolling Stones guitarist; Sidcup Art College is the art-school line in his case. Andrew Loog Oldham The Rolling Stones’ manager from 1963. He sold a refusal to be variety — a longer haircut, a press image — around a band that had started as a London R&B cover group. The Kinks Kinks North London group. “You Really Got Me” (1964) is a London riff that does not sound like a polite cover. Ray Davies Kinks singer and writer. The later English-village songs are a different chapter. 1964 is the sliced speaker and the riff. Dave Davies Kinks guitarist. The standard account of “You Really Got Me” is that he razor-slashed a speaker cone. Treat the hardware story as the usual one; the record is the fact. You Really Got Me Kinks single, 1964. Distorted riff, London, not Liverpool. A different violence from the Mersey smile. The Who London group, Shepherd’s Bush and the Mod circuit. Maximum R&B on the posters; auto-destruction on the stage. Not a Liverpool export. Pete Townshend Who guitarist; Ealing Art College is the art-school line. The Animals Animals Newcastle group with an R&B repertoire, later filed under the Invasion in America. The city is not London; the set list still came from American records. Dave Clark Five the Dave Clark Five DC5 Tottenham group. American television used them as the next British name after the Beatles. A beat group from north London, not Merseybeat. Dusty Springfield British pop and soul singer. She is in the Invasion years and not a beat group: a reminder that the American name flattened more than guitars. Manfred Mann London R&B and pop group (and the keyboardist they were named for). Another name on the 1964–65 bills. The Hollies Hollies Manchester group. The Invasion was not only Liverpool and London. The Yardbirds Yardbirds London R&B group. A club band that made the guitar a problem to be solved, not only a riff to be copied. The Shadows Shadows British instrumental group of the late 1950s–60s. The Vox AC30 was already a local sound before the Invasion name existed. Berry Gordy Founder of Motown. In 1964 his label was not waiting to be invaded. The Temptations Temptations Motown group. “My Girl” is 1964: a parallel American industry, not a footnote to Sullivan. My Girl Temptations / Motown single, 1964. Same year as the Sullivan appearance. The Beach Boys Beach Boys California group. Pet Sounds (1966) is the usual same-years comparison: another studio, another coast, not a British franchise. Pet Sounds Beach Boys album, 1966. Contemporaneous with the later Invasion years; not caused by them. France Gall French yé-yé singer, already a radio name in the mid-1960s. Sylvie Vartan French yé-yé singer. Evidence that “yeah-yeah” was not a British monopoly. The Tigers Japanese Group Sounds band of the mid-1960s. The Spiders Japanese Group Sounds band of the mid-1960s. The Blue Comets Blue Comets Japanese Group Sounds band of the mid-1960s. Cavern Club the Cavern Liverpool cellar club. The Beatles’ lunchtime residency is the tourist fact. The club was a room in a scene, not a cause. Crawdaddy Crawdaddy Club Richmond R&B club, early home of the Rolling Stones. London’s version of a cellar, with a different set list. Marine Broadcasting Offences Act 1967 British law that made supplying the pirate ships an offence. The records did not go back in the box. New Musical Express NME British weekly music paper. One of the teen and trade presses that treated beat groups as a weekly serial. Melody Maker British weekly music paper, older than NME. The other half of the London trade press the Invasion groups had to live in. Before Rationing’s aftertaste, a cheap kit, and other people’s records Postwar Britain did not jump from the Blitz to Carnaby Street. Food rationing lasted into the 1950s; meat came off the ration in 1954. What followed was not sudden luxury. It was a narrower fact: a generation that had more pocket money than its parents at the same age, and not enough official culture that sounded like it belonged to them. The BBC’s Light Programme carried pop. It did not carry enough of it. Needle-time agreements limited recorded music on air. If you wanted more than the official dose, you needed a radio that was not polite, a shop that imported American 45s, or — later — a ship that was not in British waters yet. The records arrived first. Rhythm and blues and rock and roll came as merchant-seamen singles, as classified imports, as the B-sides of things the Light Programme did not love. Chuck Berry’s “Johnny B. Goode” was a 1958 Chess single from Chicago. Little Richard, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, and the Motown 45s were the rest of the homework. In Britain they were not yet a museum. They were what you learned if you wanted a group. Chuck Berry, late-1950s publicity photograph. British beat groups did not invent this stance. They learned it from records and from the few U.S. package tours that reached them. Chuck Berry in a tuxedo, crouched, playing a Gibson electric guitar. Chess 1691, “Johnny B. Goode,” 1958. The label is the object: Chicago, two and a half minutes, C. Berry. A decade later British groups were still arguing about who owned the riff. Blue Chess Records 45 label for Johnny B. Goode by Chuck Berry, catalog 1691. Skiffle made the homework cheap. Lonnie Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” — a Lead Belly song, recorded in London — became a British hit in 1955–56. A washboard and a tea-chest bass were enough to start. John Lennon’s Quarrymen were a skiffle band. So were half the people who later grew fringes in Liverpool, London, and Manchester. Art schools did a related job: Liverpool College of Art, Ealing, Sidcup, the London colleges that Pete Townshend, Keith Richards, and others passed through. They were not conservatories. They were rooms where looking hard was a skill and a group could be a project. Lonnie Donegan, Cash Box, 23 June 1956 — the paper’s joke is that he is “riding” the Rock Island Line. The useful fact is the date: skiffle as a British hit, a cheap kit, before any American name for what came next. Lonnie Donegan in a 1956 Cash Box publicity photograph, riding the Rock Island Line as a caption joke. By the early 1960s the scenes were local before they were a national story. Liverpool had the Cavern Club and a density of beat groups later tagged Merseybeat. London had the Marquee, the Crawdaddy, and an R&B circuit that treated Chess as scripture. Manchester had the Hollies. Newcastle had the Animals. Tottenham had the Dave Clark Five. None of this required an American name yet. It required halls, managers, and a BBC that still could not play the records as often as the rooms wanted them. The era How a scene became an American headline What Americans later called the British Invasion was, from Britain, several overlapping facts. Beat groups filled ballrooms and package tours. Merseybeat and London R&B were not the same accent: Liverpool sold harmony and a smile that television could use; London’s R&B clubs sold Chess covers and a longer haircut. The look traveled with the singles. Mods, Italian suits, scooters, then Carnaby Street as a boutique strip a tourist could photograph. Teen papers — New Musical Express, Melody Maker, and the American fan magazines that followed — treated the groups as a weekly serial. The industry underneath was not a cottage. Parlophone, Decca, EMI, managers such as Brian Epstein and Andrew Loog Oldham, producers such as George Martin: large companies and a few intermediaries who had learned that a cellar residency could be a product. A mid-1960s transistor radio. The Invasion needed ships and television, but it also needed a private speaker a teenager could hold. The BBC was a household set. This was a pocket. Black portable Orion eight-transistor radio with a gold speaker grille. The American date is easy to point at and easy to over-weight. Capitol issued the Beatles’ “I Want to Hold Your Hand” in the United States in late December 1963. On 9 February 1964 they played The Ed Sullivan Show. After that, U.S. charts and variety television filled with British names: the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, the Who, the Animals, the Dave Clark Five, Dusty Springfield, Manfred Mann, the Hollies, the Yardbirds. “British Invasion” is what American radio called those months. From London the same spring, Radio Caroline began broadcasting from a ship. The BBC still had a needle-time problem. The cameras and the pirates were answering the same shortage from different sides of the ocean. MV Caroline, the first Radio Caroline ship. The station began broadcasting in March 1964 from international waters. It was a business and a workaround: records the BBC would not play in bulk, aimed at the same teenagers who were about to watch Sullivan. The ship Caroline at sea, name painted on the bow, masts and a dark funnel against a pale sky. A Vox AC30 Twin, the British amp on a lot of Invasion stages. The tag in this photograph guesses at a Shadows connection. Treat the guess as a guess. The hardware is the fact: 30 watts, two speakers, a sound that is not a Fender. A worn Vox AC30 Twin guitar amplifier with diamond grille cloth and a handwritten museum tag. The field Many names, three ways in A gallery of three faces is the wrong picture. The field is crowded on purpose. The Beatles, the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, the Who, the Animals, the Dave Clark Five, Dusty Springfield, Manfred Mann, the Hollies, the Yardbirds — and behind them the American records they learned: Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Motown, Chess. Epstein and Oldham sold the dates. Martin and the Decca that said no are the industry’s two hands. Donegan is the cheap kit. Sullivan is the American camera. Name them, then slow down for only a few, as examples inside the scene, not as the scene. The Beatles are the door. Liverpool, Hamburg, the Cavern Club, then Parlophone. This capsule does not need another press shot of four men in suits. The useful facts are the repertoire and the timing. They had already learned Berry, Little Richard, and the girl-group records. “I Want to Hold Your Hand” was a song American radio could not file as a foreign novelty for long. After Sullivan, every other British group on an American bill was walking through a door they had not cut. That is not the same as saying the others were copies. It is a fact about cameras and charts. The Rolling Stones are the R&B debt left audible. London clubs, Chess covers, Jagger and Richards, Oldham’s refusal to package them as variety. They did not invent Muddy Waters. They declined, longer than was polite, to pretend the covers were a phase. When they wrote their own songs, the debt was still the point: a British group selling America a Chicago idea with white faces on the same variety shows that had not booked the Chess roster as pop. The honest version does not scold them for learning. It keeps the label in the shot. The Kinks are a different London violence. “You Really Got Me,” 1964: Ray Davies and Dave Davies, a riff that does not behave like a cover, a speaker cone that the usual story says was sliced so the guitar would break up. Liverpool’s export was blend. This was a two-chord shove from Muswell Hill. It is one record, not a theory of the decade. It is enough to stop the Invasion from being told as four smiles and a Sullivan curtain. Elsewhere The same years, not a seating chart In Detroit, Motown under Berry Gordy was already a finished system — writers, a house band, a finishing school for movement. The Temptations’ “My Girl” is 1964. In Memphis, Stax was cutting Southern soul with a biracial house band. In California the Beach Boys were in the studio; Pet Sounds, in 1966, is the comparison the syllabuses never let go. In France, yé-yé — France Gall, Sylvie Vartan — was already a word. In Japan, Group Sounds bands (the Tigers, the Spiders, the Blue Comets) were taking electric guitars into a market that had its own kayōkyoku tradition. Britain was not the only place the 45 rpm single was rewriting a generation. It was the place American television decided to point the camera. That is a fact about power, not a ranking of songs. After Psychedelia, and the name that stopped fitting By 1966–67 the useful Invasion story — verse, chorus, suit, scream — was already too small. Revolver, then Sgt. Pepper, then a lot of other people’s sitars and tape loops. The door toward psychedelia is not a British monopoly; San Francisco is in the same late decade. The name “British Invasion” stays useful as a 1964–65 American chart event. It is a poor name for everything that happened next. The Marine Broadcasting Offences Act arrived in 1967. Radio 1 began the same year. The pirates were legislated against. The records did not go back in the box. A question Leave this on the table If a country sells another country its own music, who is the inventor in the room? The Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show (9 February 1964) Sullivan’s own site on the broadcast. Full performances are licensed; this is the historical record of the date, not a bootleg film. Chuck Berry — Johnny B. Goode (1958) Chess single 1691. The record many British groups learned from. Official/label upload; if it moves, search the title on the label’s channel. The Beatles — I Want to Hold Your Hand (1963) The Capitol single that opened the U.S. door in late 1963 / early 1964. Official Beatles channel. The Kinks — You Really Got Me (1964) Official audio. Distorted riff, London, not Liverpool. The Temptations — My Girl (1964) Motown, same year as the Sullivan appearance. Not a footnote — a parallel industry. Radio Caroline The station still exists. The 1964 ship is history; the site is the living remnant, not a 1964 tape.

subject: feminism
title: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): who got to count as a “woman” in public
dek: Suffrage, splits, and the people the word “we” left out.
text: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): who got to count as a “woman” in public Suffrage, splits, and the people the word “we” left out. c. 1848–1920 “First wave” is a later Anglo-American label, not a name the people in this capsule used for themselves. It is useful as a frame — a span of public fights over whether women counted as political persons — and incomplete as a history. What follows uses the frame, then looks at the same decades elsewhere. Feminism feminism 1848 Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments; the vote among other grievances. 1851 Akron Sojourner Truth speaks. The famous refrain is a later rewrite. 1870 The split Fifteenth Amendment: race, not sex. Stanton and Anthony versus Stone and Douglass. 1907 Anqing Qiu Jin executed after the uprising. Same decade as British militancy, different state. 1913 Procession / Derby Washington, D.C. on 3 March; Emily Wilding Davison dies at Epsom. 1920 Nineteenth Amendment The vote, and Jim Crow still standing in the way. She copyrighted the shadow In 1864 Sojourner Truth registered the copyright on her own cartes-de-visite in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan — unusual for a sitter; the photographer usually claimed the image. The cards were printed “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She sold them at lectures because lectures did not pay enough. The existing portrait in this capsule is one of those cards. coverture English common-law doctrine that a married woman’s legal identity was “covered” by her husband’s. Property, contracts, and wages were his unless a statute carved out an exception. separate spheres A nineteenth-century middle-class story: men in public/economic life, women in the home as a moral climate. It was a class rule as much as a sex rule. Wage-earning and enslaved women were never offered that delicacy. Seneca Falls Village in western New York. On 19–20 July 1848 a convention there issued the Declaration of Sentiments. “Seneca Falls” later became shorthand for the start of organized U.S. women’s rights — a useful date, not the only origin. Declaration of Sentiments Sentiments The 1848 Seneca Falls text, modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It listed grievances including the vote. The vote was not the only demand, and not everyone in the room wanted it named first. Fifteenth Amendment 15th Amendment Ratified 1870. It barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. The omission split the U.S. women’s-rights coalition. WSPU Women’s Social and Political Union Women’s Social and Political Union, founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. The militant wing of British suffrage: window-breaking, hunger strikes, and, in reply, force-feeding. Jim Crow The system of legal racial segregation and disenfranchisement in the U.S. South after Reconstruction — poll taxes, literacy tests, violence. The Nineteenth Amendment did not repeal it. 中國女報 Chinese Women’s Journal Chinese Women’s Journal, edited by Qiu Jin in Shanghai in 1907. Two issues appeared. It argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same breath as anti-Qing politics. carte-de-visite cartes-de-visite A small albumen photograph mounted on card, cheap to reproduce, sold and collected in the 1860s. Sojourner Truth sold hers with a printed caption and a copyright in her own name. Gage Frances Dana Gage Frances Dana Gage. In 1863 she published a version of Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech that includes the refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. Nineteenth Amendment 19th Amendment Ratified 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not touch poll taxes, literacy tests, or the violence that still blocked many Black women in the South. force-feeding In British prisons, hunger-striking suffragettes were restrained and fed through a tube. The Liberal government presented it as medical care. Militants presented it as assault. Both descriptions circulated in the press. doldrums A later weather report for U.S. organized feminism in the 1920s–1950s: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. It describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended. Alice Paul American suffrage organizer, trained with British militants, then with Lucy Burns planned the 3 March 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington. Later the National Woman’s Party and the Equal Rights Amendment. Before Covered, separate, and already in training English common law treated a married woman as legally covered by her husband. The doctrine is called coverture. Her property, her contracts, her wages — the law did not see a separate person there. A single woman had more legal room; marriage closed it. Industrial work left the house. What remained, for middle-class white women, was a story about respectability: the home as a moral climate, the woman as domestic, delicate, and good. Historians call this “separate spheres.” It was a rule of class as much as of sex. Enslaved women, and women who worked for wages, were never offered that delicacy. They were already in public — as labor, as property, as exceptions the ideology did not have to explain. Abolition was the school many United States feminists came out of. They learned to petition, to lecture, to edit, to organize a room. The skills transferred. The alliance later cracked, when the question became which emancipation would be allowed to go first. The era A public “we,” and the people it could not hold In 1848, at Seneca Falls, New York, a convention issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. The vote was among the grievances — not the only one, and not, at first, the one everyone in the room wanted named. The document still did something plain: it put women into the grammar of rights. A 1908 souvenir “Our Roll of Honor,” printed sixty years after Seneca Falls, listing the women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton head the first column. This is a commemorative card, not the 1848 manuscript. Printed souvenir card titled Our Roll of Honor, listing women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. In 1851 Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 rewrite of that speech. Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. The later version is the one that traveled. The historical point does not depend on the catchphrase. A feminism built on white middle-class delicacy treats enslaved women and working women as exceptions — bodies that have already been asked to do too much to count as the “woman” the movement is picturing. After the Civil War the coalition split over the Fifteenth Amendment (1870), which barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed ratifying without women. Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. The argument was about sequence, and about who was being asked to stand aside. In Britain the movement divided by method: constitutional suffragists on one side, the militant Women’s Social and Political Union — Emmeline Pankhurst’s WSPU — on the other. Hunger strikes. Force-feeding. In 1913 Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby. Emmeline Pankhurst in 1913, the year Davison died at Epsom and the WSPU’s militancy was impossible to ignore. Constitutional suffragists were still collecting signatures. Pankhurst’s organization was collecting prison time. Formal seated portrait of Emmeline Pankhurst, 1913. On 3 March 1913, the day before Wilson’s inauguration, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized the Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C. Inez Milholland rode in white on a white horse. Ida B. Wells was told that Black women should march in a rear contingent. She refused, and stepped into the Illinois delegation as it passed. The crowd on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913. Men climbed poles and wagons to see. The procession was designed to be unmissable on the eve of an inauguration. Unmissable is not the same as welcomed: the parade was repeatedly broken by spectators stepping into the street. A dense crowd lining Pennsylvania Avenue to watch the 1913 woman suffrage procession in Washington, D.C. The official program for the same day. The horse, the banner, the Capitol: a picture of who the procession wanted to look like. Wells’s decision to leave the “rear contingent” is the part the program does not print. Color official program cover for the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913, showing a woman on horseback before the Capitol. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. It did not undo Jim Crow. Many Black women in the South were still blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence. The amendment changed the federal text. The ground did not change with it. The same years, elsewhere: Qiu Jin 秋瑾 (1875–1907). She unbound her feet, studied in Japan, edited 中國女報 (the Chinese Women’s Journal), and was executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. Her public life does not sit on the Anglo-American staircase from Seneca Falls to 1920. It belongs in the same decades anyway — a woman deciding she would count in public, under a different state, and paying for it. People Four lives the frame has to stretch for Sojourner Truth c. 1797–1883 Born enslaved in New York. She sold cartes-de-visite captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” The card was a living. It was also an argument about who owned the image of a woman who had been treated as property. Carte-de-visite, 1864. “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” Ida B. Wells 1862–1931 Anti-lynching journalist; Southern Horrors appeared in 1892. She treated suffrage and racial terror as one fight, which is why a segregated parade order was not a small slight. She walked into the Illinois line instead. Ida B. Wells-Barnett, photograph by Mary Garrity, c. 1893. Inez Milholland 1886–1916 Lawyer and the image the 1913 procession needed at its head. She died in 1916 on a western suffrage tour, at thirty. The photograph outlived the campaign she was riding for. The 1913 visual: white cape, white horse, Pennsylvania Avenue. Qiu Jin 秋瑾 1875–1907 Unbound feet. Study in Japan. Editor of 中國女報. Executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. If “first wave” cannot hold her, the phrase is too small — not her life. Qiu Jin, photographed between 1900 and 1907. A story The shadow and the substance Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it. Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait. Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. The “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold. Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject, and which body is the illustration. After The vote, the doldrums, and the staircase In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. The word is a weather report written after the fact. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended. What gets called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, to housework. “The personal is political.” The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues. The wave metaphor itself is the after. It offers a tidy staircase: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never on the stairs — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered swell. A question Leave this on the table When a movement says “we,” who is being asked to wait? Time to Remember — Time of the Suffragettes (1911–1913) British Pathé compilation of British suffragette newsreel, 1911–1913. This is not film of the 1913 Washington procession. The Derby — 1912 & 1913 British Pathé racing newsreel. It includes the 1913 Epsom Derby, when Emily Wilding Davison stepped onto the course. Again: Britain, not Pennsylvania Avenue.
